title: Akkadians
titleline: Akkadians - The History Web
para1: The Akkadian Empire was the world's first multinational empire, centered on the city of Akkad, somewhere along the Euphrates in what is now Iraq; the city's exact site has never been found. Rising to power around 2334 BCE under the legendary Sargon the Great, it united the Akkadian and Sumerian speaking cities of Mesopotamia under a single rule for the first time on such a scale. It matters because Sargon set the model that later Mesopotamian kings would follow or strive to surpass: his own inscriptions boast that he secured access to all the major trade routes, by sea and by land.
para2: Sargon was not quite the first unifier: Lugalzagesi of Uruk had subdued the cities of Sumer before him, but on a smaller scale, and Sargon improved on that model to build something larger and stronger. Under his dynasty, Akkadian replaced Sumerian as the everyday language of rule and letters, except in sacred services, and it remained the common tongue of the Near East long after the empire itself was dust.
para3: Empire was heavy handed work: Sargon's successors spent enormous effort crushing revolts, and later generations remembered kings like Sargon and Naram-Sin in poems and myths as great but flawed figures, brutal in suppressing any dissent. After the reign of Shar-Kali-Sharri the dynasty frayed into civil war, with four men fighting for the throne in quick succession, and central authority collapsed around 2154 BCE.
para4: Yet the idea of Akkad never died: the Sumerian kings of Ur III consciously followed Sargon's example, and the Assyrian kings of the next millennium took him as their prototype, the image on which they modeled their own ambitions. The first empire lasted barely two centuries, but every empire that came after walked the road it cut.

title: Achaemenid Empire
titleline: Achaemenid Empire - The History Web
para1: Achaemenid Empire. The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, was the largest empire the world had yet seen: at its peak it covered some 5.5 million square kilometers, from the Balkans and Egypt in the west to the Indus Valley in the east, ruling tens of millions of people. Cyrus rose from Persis in southwestern Iran and in twenty years toppled three great powers - Media in 550, Croesus's Lydia in 547, and Babylon in 539 BCE, where the Cyrus Cylinder presented him as a restorer of order and where he freed the Jews from their Babylonian captivity, allowing them to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. His son Cambyses II added Egypt in 525 BCE after the battle of Pelusium.
para2: The empire's true genius was organization. Darius the Great, who seized the throne in 522 BCE amid the confusion of a royal impostor he denounced on the great Behistun Inscription, divided the realm into satrapies governed by satraps, knit it together with the Royal Road and an organized postal service, and issued the gold daric coinage. Aramaic served as the administrative lingua franca alongside Old Persian, and the kings ruled from Susa and the ceremonial splendor of Persepolis. The Achaemenids are remembered for a multicultural policy and religious tolerance unusual for their age - Zoroastrianism was the dynasty's faith, but Jews, Egyptians, Greeks, and Babylonians worshipped their own gods - and their bureaucracy, civil service, and professional army and navy became models copied by later empires.
para3: The western frontier proved the hardest. After the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE, Darius's punitive expedition was defeated at Marathon in 490; his son Xerxes I invaded Greece with an enormous army in 480, forced the pass at Thermopylae, and sacked Athens, only to lose his fleet at Salamis and his army at Plataea and Mycale in 479, after which Persia lost its European territories. Thereafter the empire managed Greece by gold rather than armies - Persian funding helped Sparta finally defeat Athens in 404 BCE - and when Cyrus the Younger marched on his brother Artaxerxes II with the famous Ten Thousand Greek mercenaries in 401, his death at Cunaxa left the Greeks the long march home that Xenophon immortalized.
para4: Artaxerxes II's 45-year reign brought stability and a building boom, but the Great Satraps' Revolt of 372-362 BCE showed the seams, and although Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt in 343, the empire's two centuries were nearing their end. Between 336 and 330 BCE Alexander of Macedon conquered the whole empire, defeating the last king, Darius III, at Gaugamela in 331. Yet the Achaemenid template - provinces, roads, coinage, tolerance, a professional administration - passed almost intact to the Seleucids, was reclaimed by the Iranian Parthians and Sasanians, and still shapes how we imagine empire itself.

title: Ammon, Edom, and Moab
titleline: Ammon, Edom, and Moab - The History Web
para1: Ammon, Edom, and Moab were three Iron Age kingdoms of the Transjordanian highlands, in what is now Jordan. Ammon occupied the plateau between the Jabbok and Arnon valleys, its capital at Rabbah, modern Amman; Moab held the mountainous country east of the Dead Sea, ruled from Dibon; and Edom stretched south of the Wadi al-Hasa, its capital at Bozrah. Their languages belonged to the Canaanite family, closely related to Hebrew, and their chief gods were Milcom, Chemosh, and Qos. They lived from farming, herding, and local resources - Edom's copper mines at Khirbat en-Nahas were among the largest in the region - and above all from the King's Highway, the trade route connecting Egypt with Mesopotamia and Syria, whose tolls gave all three considerable revenue.
para2: The Hebrew Bible portrays the three as kin and rivals of Israel: Ammonites and Moabites as descendants of Lot, Edomites of Esau. In the biblical account, the Ammonite king Nahash's siege of Jabesh-Gilead spurred the Israelite tribes to unify under Saul, and David later conquered the Ammonite cities, made Moab tributary, and defeated Edom in the Valley of Salt, though Moab also appears in friendlier tradition through Ruth, the Moabite great-grandmother of David. After Ahab's death around 853 BCE, King Mesha of Moab rebelled: the Bible claims an Israelite victory, but Mesha's own inscription, the famous Mesha Stele, claims complete victory and the recovery of every town Israel had taken - a rare case where both sides of an ancient war survive in their own words. Edom, whose king list Genesis places 'before any king reigned over the Israelites', passed from vassalage under David to revolt under Jehoram.
para3: When the Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded into the Levant, all three chose tribute over annexation. The Kurkh Monolith lists the Ammonite king Baasha ben Ruhubi fighting alongside Ahab against Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BCE, and an Assyrian tribute list shows Ammon paying one-fifth of Judah's tribute. Moab's king Salmanu appears among the tributaries of Tiglath-Pileser III, and Moabite and Edomite emissaries received wine rations at the Assyrian court of Nimrud; Edom's kings are known almost entirely from such Assyrian records. In 711 BCE Moab joined Edom and Judah in a coalition against Sargon II yet escaped the devastation visited on Ashdod, and vassalage had its uses: Assyrian support shielded the Transjordanian kingdoms from the nomadic tribes of the Arabian desert.
para4: The Babylonian period ended their independence. Nebuchadnezzar II devastated Ammon in the 580s BCE and made it a province, though archaeology shows Ammon actually flourished under Babylonian and Persian rule, overturning the older view of a desolate Transjordan. Edom was destroyed in the 6th century BCE, its people pushed westward by nomads, among them the Nabataeans, who built their kingdom in former Edomite territory; the Edomites settled in southern Judah as the people Greeks and Romans called Idumeans, absorbed into the Jewish population by the 2nd century BCE - Herod the Great was of Edomite origin. Moab faded from the record after aiding Nebuchadnezzar against Judah, while Ammonites were still a numerous people in the 2nd century CE, the last notice of the three nations.

title: Assyria & the Neo-Assyrian Empire
titleline: Assyria & the Neo-Assyrian Empire - The History Web
para1: Assyria was the region of the ancient Near East that grew into one of the most effective military powers in history, dominating the Middle East under the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 912 to 612 BCE. It began modestly at the city of Ashur in northern Mesopotamia, whose merchants grew wealthy trading in Anatolia; the city took its name from the god Ashur, and the land from the city. Subjugated by Hammurabi of Babylon around 1792 BCE, Assyria reasserted itself after his empire fell apart, and by the 13th century BCE Tukulti-Ninurta I could defeat the Hittites at the Battle of Nihriya and sack Babylon itself. In the 11th century BCE Tiglath Pileser I revitalized the kingdom, and his care for preserving cuneiform tablets became the model for Ashurbanipal's famous library.
para2: The Assyrian army became the most effective military force in history up to that time and a model for future armies in organization, tactics, and training; the Assyrians were the first to make extensive use of iron weaponry, which could be mass-produced to equip very large armies. Tiglath Pileser III (745-727 BCE) reorganized the military, replacing conscription with a manpower levy imposed on each province and demanding contingents from vassal states, reconquered the Mediterranean seaboard, and subjugated Babylon. Sargon II founded the final Sargonid dynasty, Sennacherib moved the capital to Nineveh and built 'the Palace without a Rival', and Esarhaddon conquered Egypt.
para3: The last great king, Ashurbanipal (668-627 BCE), assembled at Nineveh the largest collection of cuneiform tablets in the world at that time, preserving the written works of Mesopotamia, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Conquered peoples were relocated in mass deportations, scribes and scholars chosen carefully and sent to urban centres to serve the bureaucracy. The empire's reputation was fearsome: one historian wrote that Assyria must surely have among the worst press notices of any state in history.
para4: That resentment caught up with them. When Ashurbanipal died in 627 BCE, revolts broke out across the empire, and over the next fifteen years Medes, Babylonians, Persians, Cimmerians, Scythians, and Chaldeans sacked the Assyrian cities. In 612 BCE Nineveh, Ashur, and Kalhu were destroyed, and the empire dissolved. Ashurbanipal's library was buried beneath the burning walls of his palace, but the fire only hardened its clay tablets, preserving them until the excavations of Layard and Rassam and the translations of George Smith brought them to light in the 19th century.

title: Babylonians & the Neo-Babylonian Empire
titleline: Babylonians & the Neo-Babylonian Empire - The History Web
para1: Babylon was an ancient cultural and political powerhouse on the Euphrates in modern Iraq, famously rising to prominence twice. Long a small but profitable river port under an Amorite dynasty from around 1894 BCE, its first peak came under Hammurabi (reign 1792-1750 BCE), who quietly built and trained an army, seized Isin and Uruk from his overlords in Larsa, and by 1755 BCE had united all of Mesopotamia. Babylon was by then the largest city in the world, with a population estimated at over 200,000, and so famous that all of southern Mesopotamia came to be called Babylonia. His Code of around 1772 BCE is one of the earliest law codes in the world, and he paired it with heightened walls, temples, and canals.
para2: After Hammurabi's death his empire fell apart: the Hittites sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE, and the Kassites ruled Babylonia for over four centuries. The great ziggurat Etemenanki, begun sometime between the 14th and 9th centuries BCE, was later associated with the biblical Tower of Babel through a misreading of the Akkadian bav-il, Gate of the Gods, as the Hebrew bavel, confusion. When Babylon kept revolting under Assyrian rule, King Sennacherib had it razed in 689 BCE, an act seen as so impious that his own sons assassinated him; his successor Esarhaddon rebuilt the city.
para3: After the Assyrian Empire fell, the Chaldean king Nabopolassar founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 626 BCE. His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605/604-562 BCE) renovated Babylon until it covered some 900 hectares, captured Jerusalem in 597 BCE, and began the Babylonian captivity of the Jews. His building program gave the city its famous image: the immense walls and the Ishtar Gate around 575 BCE, the completed Etemenanki, and, according to later Greek writers, the Hanging Gardens, though recent scholarship argues those were actually Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh, since no trace of them has been found at Babylon.
para4: The glory was spectacular but brief. In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great defeated the Babylonian army at Opis, and the Persians entered the impregnable city after diverting the Euphrates to a manageable depth. Under Persian rule Babylon flourished as a center of art and education, its mathematics and astronomy so respected that Thales of Miletus is thought to have studied there and Pythagoras to have drawn his theorem from a Babylonian model. The city passed to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE and remained a trade center under later empires, but never regained the heights it had known under Hammurabi or Nebuchadnezzar II.

title: Cimmerians
titleline: Cimmerians - The History Web
para1: Cimmerians. The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, culturally Scythian but politically distinct from the Scythians proper, their relatives who eventually displaced them. They left no writings of their own: almost everything known about them comes from Neo-Assyrian intelligence reports of the 8th-7th centuries BCE, which called them Gimirri, and from later Greek authors, who knew them as Kimmerioi. They were among the first true nomads of the steppe, born of climatic changes around the start of the 1st millennium BCE that turned former farmers into mounted herders.
para2: Pressed by the expanding Scythians, part of the Cimmerians crossed the Caucasus into West Asia in the late 8th century BCE, raiding through the kingdom of Mannai. Their first dated appearance is spectacular: Assyrian reports of 714 BCE record that they crushed a counter-attack by Rusa I of Urartu, capturing his commanders and so weakening that great kingdom that the Assyrian king Sargon II defeated it the same year. In Anatolia they terrified the established powers - King Midas of Phrygia, once Assyria's bitter enemy, sought an anti-Cimmerian alliance with Sargon in 709 BCE - and in 705 BCE Sargon II himself was killed in battle campaigning in Tabal, probably against Cimmerian forces.
para3: Through the 7th century BCE the bulk of the Cimmerians operated in Anatolia, and the disturbances they caused let many local rulers slip free of Assyrian overlordship. Their high point came in 644 BCE, when the Cimmerians and their Treres allies defeated the Lydians and captured Sardis, one of the richest capitals of the age. It could not last: around 635 BCE the Scythians under Madyes, acting with Assyrian approval, entered Anatolia and crushed the Cimmerians alongside the resurgent Lydians, and the survivors faded from the records soon after.
para4: The Cimmerians vanished as a people, absorbed into the populations they had once terrorized, but their name refused to die: Late Babylonian scribes of the Persian Empire went on calling every steppe nomad people 'Gimirri', Scythians and Saka included, long after the real Cimmerians were gone. Their brief, violent passage across West Asia - shattering Urartu's power, helping topple Phrygia's order, taking Sardis - permanently reshuffled the politics of the region, weakening the old kingdoms just as Assyria and then the Medes and Persians rose to dominate it.

title: Elam
titleline: Elam - The History Web
para1: Elam. Elam was an ancient civilization centered in the far west and southwest of modern Iran, from the Khuzestan lowlands to the Zagros highlands around Anshan, known to classical writers as Susiana after its capital, Susa, one of the oldest cities in the world. The Elamite language was an isolate, unrelated to Sumerian, to the Semitic languages, or to the Iranian tongues that came later, and the still-undeciphered proto-Elamite script, appearing around 3000 BCE, ranks among humanity's earliest writing. For more than two thousand years, Elamite states stood among the leading powers of the ancient Near East, astride the routes connecting the Iranian plateau to the cities of Mesopotamia.
para2: Elamite history, reconstructed mostly from Mesopotamian records, was a constant contest with its western neighbors. Sargon of Akkad defeated the Elamite king of Awan and tried to impose the Akkadian language; Elam threw off Akkadian rule under Kutik-Inshushinak, and in 2004 BCE the Elamites under Kindattu sacked Ur itself, ending the Third Dynasty of Ur. In the Sukkalmah period, Elam's 'great kings' were addressed as 'Father' by the rulers of Mesopotamia, including the young Hammurabi - who around 1760 BCE drove the Elamites out and built his own short-lived Babylonian empire. Etched carnelian beads and Indus seals found at Susa show Elam's trade reaching as far as the Indus Valley.
para3: Elam's golden age came in the Middle Elamite period (c. 1500-1100 BCE), when its kings took the title 'king of Anshan and Susa'. King Untash Napirisha raised the great ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil around 1250 BCE, today the best preserved in the world. Under the Shutrukid dynasty the empire reached its height: Shutruk-Nakhkhunte raided Babylonia and carried home trophies including the Stele of Naram-Sin and the very stele bearing Hammurabi's law code - which is why those Mesopotamian masterpieces were found at Susa - and in 1158 BCE the Elamites destroyed Kassite power permanently, briefly placing one of their own on Babylon's throne.
para4: Elam's last centuries were spent resisting the Neo-Assyrian Empire as Babylon's ally. Ashurbanipal broke Elamite power at the battle of Ulai in 653 BCE, sacked Susa in 646, and by 640 had captured the last Elamite king, Humban-Haltash III, annexing and destroying the kingdom. Yet Elam's legacy outlived its state: Persian settlers under Teispes took over Anshan, making it the nucleus of the future Achaemenid dynasty, Elam's administrative traditions became a foundation of Iranian government, and Susa went on to serve as a royal capital of the Persian kings.

title: Indus Valley Civilization
titleline: Indus Valley Civilization - The History Web
para1: Indus Valley Civilization. The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilization after its first excavated city, was one of the four great cradles of the ancient world - and in sheer area the largest, spreading over a million square kilometers of what is now Pakistan, northwest India, and northeast Afghanistan, larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. It flourished along the Indus River and the now-faded Ghaggar-Hakra river system from about 3300 to 1300 BCE, reaching its mature phase between 2600 and 1900 BCE, when its population may have numbered between one and five million people.
para2: Its cities were unlike anything else in the Bronze Age: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each home to perhaps 30,000-60,000 people, were laid out on planned grids with baked-brick houses, covered drains, wells, and sophisticated water supply - urban sanitation unmatched until the Romans. Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath and massive granaries speak of organized civic life, yet strikingly, archaeologists have found no obvious palaces, temples, or royal tombs, leaving the question of who ruled these cities unanswered to this day.
para3: The Harappans were masters of craft and commerce: their standardized weights, bead-making, and metalwork were exported across the ancient world, and Indus seals and etched carnelian beads have been dug up in Mesopotamia, whose texts speak of a trading land called Meluhha - almost certainly the Indus. They wrote in a script of some 400 signs stamped on thousands of seals, but with no bilingual text and inscriptions only a few symbols long, the Indus script remains undeciphered and their language unknown, though many scholars favor a connection to the Dravidian family.
para4: Around 1900 BCE the cities began to empty. The leading explanation is not invasion but climate: a gradual drying of the region shrank the rivers that fed Harappan agriculture, and the population drifted eastward into smaller rural communities, carrying pieces of their old world with them. The civilization vanished so completely that when Harappa's ruins were first recorded in the 19th century they were mistaken for a city of Alexander's time; only the excavations of the 1920s revealed that South Asia had nursed a civilization as old and as grand as Egypt's - one whose people we can see but whose words we still cannot read.

title: Maurya Empire
titleline: Maurya Empire - The History Web
para1: Maurya Empire. The Maurya Empire was the first power to unite most of the Indian subcontinent under one rule. Founded around 321 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha and built his capital at Pataliputra, near modern Patna, the empire was guided in its early years by his brilliant adviser Kautilya, to whom tradition attributes the Arthashastra, the great ancient treatise on statecraft. When Alexander's successor Seleucus I tried to reclaim the Indus lands in 305 BCE, Chandragupta defeated him and traded him the territories for alliance and five hundred war elephants; under Chandragupta's son Bindusara the empire pushed into the Deccan.
para2: The empire reached its height under Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE), who ruled everything from Afghanistan to the Bay of Bengal except the deep south - a realm of perhaps 15 to 30 million people. The conquest of Kalinga in 261 BCE was so bloody that, by his own account, it broke something in him: Ashoka embraced Buddhism and nonviolence, and spread his new ethic across the empire in rock and pillar edicts written in the people's own languages - among the earliest deciphered texts in Indian history. He sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, and beyond, a key reason Buddhism became a world religion.
para3: Mauryan government was remarkably sophisticated for its age: a centralized administration, roads like the great Uttarapatha highway linking Afghanistan to the Ganges, coinage, state-supported agriculture, and a capital described by the Greek ambassador Megasthenes, whose lost account long shaped the world's picture of India. It was also an age of striking creativity in art and architecture - the polished sandstone pillars crowned with animal capitals are its signature - though scholars note the period also saw caste harden and women's rights decline in the Indo-Aryan heartland.
para4: The empire did not long outlive Ashoka. His weaker successors lost the provinces piecemeal, and in 185 BCE the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, was assassinated by his own general Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga dynasty. The Mauryas left two legacies still visible today: the idea of a united India, and Ashoka himself - whose lion capital at Sarnath became the emblem of the modern Indian republic, and whose wheel of dharma turns at the center of its flag.

title: Philistines
titleline: Philistines - The History Web
para1: The Philistines were a people of Aegean origin who settled the southern coast of Canaan in the 12th century BCE, about the time the Israelites were emerging inland. They first appear in history on the walls of the mortuary temple of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu, among the Sea Peoples who invaded Egypt about 1190 BCE after ravaging Anatolia, Cyprus, and Syria; repulsed by the Egyptians, they settled, possibly with Egypt's permission, on the coastal plain from Joppa down to Gaza.
para2: There they formed a confederacy of five cities, the Pentapolis: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath, a land called Philistia, from which the Greeks would eventually name the whole country Palestine. Biblical tradition says they came from Caphtor, perhaps Crete, and their archaeology backs an Aegean connection: their early pottery follows Mycenaean styles, and their excavated temples at Ashdod, Ekron, and Tel Qasile show Aegean design.
para3: The Philistines matter as the great rivals of the early Israelites: around 1050 BCE their superior arms and organization let them occupy part of the Judaean hill country, and their local monopoly on iron smithing, a skill probably acquired in Anatolia, gave them a military edge remembered in the Bible's complaint that no smith could be found in Israel. The struggle echoes through the Bible's Samson saga, and it was the Israelite king David who, in the biblical account, finally broke their power in the 10th century.
para4: After David, their history became that of individual cities rather than a people: they paid tribute to the Assyrian king Adad-nirari III in the 8th century BCE, passed from Assyrian to Egyptian vassalage in the 7th, and became part of Nebuchadnezzar's Neo-Babylonian empire. The cities later passed under Persian, Greek, and Roman control, while the Philistines themselves faded as a distinct people - their language replaced by Canaanite, Aramaic, and later Greek - leaving only their name on the land.

title: Phoenician City-States
titleline: Phoenician City-States - The History Web
para1: The Phoenician City-States were independent coastal trading hubs strung along modern Lebanon, cities like Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos, bound by a shared language and culture rather than united in an empire. Their cities began to take form as early as 3200 BCE, and Phoenicia thrived as a maritime trader and manufacturing center from about 1500 to 332 BCE, famed for shipbuilding, glass making, and luxury goods of every kind.
para2: Their signature product was the purple dye of Tyre, extracted from murex snails, which became the standard adornment of royalty from Mesopotamia to Rome; the Greeks named the whole people for it, Phoinikes, the purple people, and said the dye stained the workers' skin. Sidon was so skilled in glass that later ages thought its people had invented it, and Phoenician workshops seem to have pioneered mass production, turning out near identical goods for markets across the sea.
para3: The Phoenicians' greatest gift was the alphabet: Herodotus names Phoenicia as its birthplace, carried to Greece by the Phoenician Kadmus, and their script is the ancestor of most western alphabets today. Even the word Bible runs through them: their city of Byblos exported so much Egyptian papyrus that the Greeks called books ta biblia after it, and Byblos was where the curved hull of seagoing ships was first perfected.
para4: Where they traded, they settled: their colonies dotted the Mediterranean, with Carthage in North Africa becoming the most famous and powerful, and as carriers of other nations' goods they became the ancient world's great middlemen of culture. Greater empires dominated them in turn, and in 332 BCE Alexander the Great besieged and took island Tyre, after which the region turned steadily toward Hellenism.

title: Shang Dynasty
titleline: Shang Dynasty - The History Web
para1: Shang Dynasty. The Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) ruled the Yellow River valley as Bronze Age China's first confirmed historical dynasty - the earliest line of Chinese kings we can name, date, and verify, because they left us their own words. Where the Xia survives only in later tradition, the Shang survives in bronze, bone, and earth: the oracle bone inscriptions, the oldest Chinese writing, record the divinations of kings whom Sima Qian's much later king list names almost exactly, proving the ancient historians right.
para2: The dynasty's heartland was the middle Yellow River, its capitals shifting until King Pan Geng settled at Yin, near modern Anyang - the 'Yinxu' site that gave the dynasty its other name. Excavations there have revealed eleven royal tombs, palace foundations, and tens of thousands of bronzes, jades, and bones. They also reveal the dynasty's grim grandeur: the Shang kings practiced divination by heating turtle shells and ox shoulder blades until they cracked, reading the cracks as answers from the ancestors, and inscribing the questions - about harvests, battles, illness, rainfall - that give us our first Chinese texts. Royal funerals were accompanied by human sacrifice on a massive scale.
para3: Shang kingship was a theocracy of ancestor worship: the king was the essential intermediary between the living and the royal ancestors, whose favor determined the fate of the harvest and the state. The dynasty reached its height under King Wu Ding (c. 1250-1191 BCE), whose consort Fu Hao - general, landowner, and high priestess - is the earliest Chinese woman whose life we can trace, her intact tomb filled with hundreds of bronzes and jades. Shang bronze-casting, the ritual vessels with their staring taotie masks, remains among the supreme achievements of the ancient world.
para4: The end, as tradition tells it, matched the pattern the Xia had set: the last king, Di Xin, was a brilliant but depraved tyrant whose excesses forfeited the Mandate of Heaven, and the rising Zhou people destroyed his army at the Battle of Muye around 1046 BCE. But the Shang's legacy is the foundation of Chinese civilization itself: writing, dynastic kingship, bronze ritual, and ancestor worship all descend from them. Every later Chinese dynasty stood on ground the Shang had laid.

title: The Funan Kingdom
titleline: The Funan Kingdom - The History Web
para1: Funan. The kingdom the Chinese called Funan was, so far as we know, the first great state of Southeast Asia: a network of Indianized trading cities centered on the Mekong Delta, flourishing from roughly the 1st to the 6th century CE across what is now southern Vietnam and Cambodia. 'Funan' is not even its real name - no local inscription uses it. It is the Chinese rendering, possibly of an old Khmer word for 'mountain', and everything we know of the kingdom comes from Chinese chronicles and from the soil itself.
para2: Chinese legend gave Funan a foundation myth: the Indian Brahmin Kaundinya, guided by a dream, sailed to the delta, defeated the local serpent-queen Soma in combat, and married her - a story that encodes the historical truth of 'Indianization'. From the early centuries CE, traders, priests, and ideas flowed across the Bay of Bengal, and Southeast Asian rulers adopted Sanskrit, Hindu and Buddhist religion, and Indian concepts of kingship, blending them with local traditions rather than replacing them.
para3: Funan's wealth came from geography. Its cities sat astride the maritime route between India and China, and its great port of Oc Eo, linked by canals to the inland capital near Angkor Borei, was one of the ancient world's busiest entrepots - excavations there have unearthed Roman coins and medallions, Indian gems, and Chinese goods, evidence of trade reaching from Rome to the Han. Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, who visited in the mid-3rd century, described a kingdom of walled cities, palaces, and taxes paid in gold, silver, and pearls.
para4: From the 5th century, Funan's power waned as trade routes shifted and its upriver vassal, Chenla, grew strong in the interior; by the 7th century Chenla had absorbed its former master, and Funan faded from the record. But its template - the Indianized maritime state living from the straits trade - was inherited by Srivijaya, and its people and traditions were the ancestors of Angkor. Cambodia's royal chronicles traced their kings back to Funan's founding pair, Kaundinya and Soma.

title: The Hittites
titleline: The Hittites - The History Web
para1: The Hittite Empire was an ancient Anatolian power that dominated modern-day Turkey and northern Syria between about 1650 and 1190 BCE, ruled from its capital at Hattusa, high on the rugged central Anatolian plateau. The Hittites were an Indo-European people who settled in north-central Anatolia early in the 2nd millennium BCE and absorbed the earlier Hattian inhabitants, from whom they took the name of both their land and their capital. Older scholarship credited them with pioneering iron smelting and monopolizing ironworking, giving them an edge over bronze-wielding neighbors, but that view is now contested: Bronze Age iron objects from Anatolia are no more numerous than those from Egypt or Mesopotamia, and most appear to be meteoritic. The Hittite military did make successful use of chariots.
para2: The Hittites also developed a distinctive legal system. Under their law code, crimes such as murder and theft, which were capital offenses in other southwest Asian kingdoms, were punished mainly by restitution, with the thief repaying what was stolen. And where Egypt's pharaohs were worshipped as living gods, the early Hittite king was a first among equals; only after about 1400 BCE did the kingship become centralized and powerful.
para3: The empire reached its peak in the mid-14th century BCE under Suppiluliuma I, when it encompassed most of Anatolia, parts of northern Syria, and Upper Mesopotamia. Hittite prosperity depended on controlling trade routes and metal sources, and that brought collision with the expanding Egypt of Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE, a hard-fought clash with no clear winner. With Assyria rising as a threat to both, King Hattusili III concluded a peace and alliance with Ramesses around 1258 BCE: the Treaty of Kadesh, among the oldest surviving written peace treaties in history, sealed by the marriage of a Hittite princess to the pharaoh.
para4: In the end it was Assyria and new migrating peoples that broke the kingdom. Much of the empire was annexed by the Middle Assyrian Empire while the remainder was sacked by Phrygian newcomers, and Hattusa itself was abandoned around 1190 BCE during the Late Bronze Age collapse. The Hittites fractured into smaller independent Syro-Hittite states, some of which survived until the 8th century BCE before succumbing to the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

title: The Island Kingdoms of Southeast Asia
titleline: The Island Kingdoms of Southeast Asia - The History Web
para1: Island Kingdoms of Southeast Asia. While mainland Southeast Asia raised its kingdoms on rivers and rice, the archipelago - the thousands of islands of modern Indonesia and Malaysia - built powers of a different kind: maritime states grown rich on the chokepoints of the spice trade. The greatest of them, Srivijaya and Majapahit, between them commanded the seas between India and China for seven hundred years.
para2: Srivijaya, centered at Palembang on Sumatra from the late 7th century, was the first power to dominate the island world. Its position straddling the Strait of Malacca - the narrow funnel through which all India-China shipping had to pass - made it the tollkeeper of the richest trade route on earth. The Chinese monk Yijing, who studied there in 671, found a devout Buddhist kingdom with more than a thousand monks, and for centuries Srivijaya was a renowned center of Buddhist learning, its kings patrons of monasteries from Sumatra to Bengal. A thalassocracy rather than a territorial state, it ruled through a web of loyal port cities whose allegiance was bought with shared profits - and enforced by fleets when persuasion failed.
para3: Srivijaya survived for six centuries, weathering invasion by the Cholas of southern India in 1025 and endless rivalry with Java, until shifting trade and Javanese pressure reduced it by the 13th century. Java then produced the archipelago's second great power: Majapahit. Founded in 1293 by Raden Wijaya - who famously turned a Mongol invasion force against his own local rivals, then drove the Mongols back to sea - Majapahit rose under the brilliant prime minister Gajah Mada and King Hayam Wuruk (reigned 1350-1389) to claim suzerainty over nearly the whole archipelago: the court poem Nagarakretagama boasts of 98 tributaries from Sumatra to New Guinea, though historians debate how real that control was beyond eastern Java.
para4: Majapahit was the last and greatest of the Hindu-Buddhist island empires. Weakened by civil war after Hayam Wuruk's death and undercut by the spread of Islam along the trade routes it depended on, it collapsed in 1527 under attack from the Islamic Sultanate of Demak; its courts and craftsmen fled east to Bali, which keeps Majapahit's Hindu culture alive today. The island kingdoms left a template - the sea-trading, religiously cosmopolitan maritime state - that Malacca and the later sultanates would inherit, and a golden age that Indonesia still claims as its own.

title: The Israelite Kingdoms
titleline: The Israelite Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Israelite Kingdoms. According to the Hebrew Bible, the tribes of Israel were first united in a single kingdom under Saul, then David (c. 1008-970 BCE), and then Solomon (c. 970-931 BCE), who built the First Temple in Jerusalem with the help of Tyrian architects and craftsmen. The first mention of Israel outside the Bible comes much earlier, on the Egyptian Merneptah Stele of 1208 BCE, but how grand the united monarchy really was is one of archaeology's fiercest debates: since the 1980s scholars like Israel Finkelstein have argued the evidence for a large 10th-century kingdom is too weak, while others, like Amihai Mazar, defend a modified version of the traditional chronology. What is certain is that by the mid-9th century BCE a 'House of David' ruled a kingdom in the south, as the Tel Dan Stele, discovered in 1993, attests.
para2: On the accession of Solomon's son Rehoboam, around 930 BCE, the northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam and the kingdom split in two: the Kingdom of Israel in the north, ruled from Shechem, then Tirzah, then Samaria, and the Kingdom of Judah in the south, ruled from Jerusalem by the House of David for four centuries. The northern kingdom was the larger and wealthier of the two, and Assyrian records knew it as the 'House of Omri': the Kurkh Monolith of 853 BCE names 'Ahab the Israelite' fighting at Qarqar, and the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III shows King Jehu bowing in tribute, the only surviving ancient Near Eastern portrait of an Israelite or Judean monarch.
para3: Both kingdoms lived in the shadow of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Tiglath-Pileser III annexed Galilee and Gilead in 732 BCE, and after a three-year siege Samaria itself fell around 720 BCE; Sargon II's own inscriptions record that he carried away 27,290 Israelites, the deportation remembered as the Assyrian captivity and the origin of the legend of the Ten Lost Tribes. In reality only a fraction of the population - perhaps a fifth - was exiled; those who remained around Mount Gerizim became the ancestors of the Samaritans, while many refugees fled south, swelling Jerusalem to perhaps five times its former size under King Hezekiah.
para4: Judah outlived its northern sister by nearly a century and a half, prospering as an Assyrian vassal in the 7th century BCE despite Hezekiah's revolt against Sennacherib, and enacting Josiah's religious reforms as Assyrian power waned. When Assyria fell in 605 BCE, Judah was caught between Egypt and the rising Neo-Babylonian Empire, and its Egyptian-backed rebellions proved fatal: in 587 BCE Nebuchadnezzar II besieged and destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, deported a large number of Judeans to Babylonia, and annexed the kingdom as a province. The Babylonian exile that followed became one of the defining chapters of Jewish history - and it is from Judah, the smaller but longer-lived kingdom, that the Jewish people take their name.

title: The Nabataean Kingdom
titleline: The Nabataean Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Nabataean Kingdom. The Nabataeans were an Arab people who began as nomads of the Arabian desert and built, by the mid-3rd century BCE, one of the most remarkable trading kingdoms of the ancient world. From their rock-carved capital at Petra, with the cities of Hegra (Mada'in Salih) in the Hejaz and Bosra in the north, they controlled the caravan routes that carried frankincense, myrrh, and spices from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean port of Gaza - and grew fabulously rich on the tolls. Their language was Arabic, their official script Aramaic, and their kingdom stretched at its zenith from the Hejaz to Damascus, which they held from 85 to 71 BCE.
para2: Their secret was water. Greek writers marveled that the Nabataeans survived in a waterless desert by digging hidden cisterns marked with signs only they could read, vanishing into the sands while invading armies died of thirst - a trick they used to annihilate the 4,000-strong raiding force the Macedonian general Antigonus sent against their rock stronghold in 312 BCE. Diodorus recorded that 'neither the Assyrians of old, nor the kings of the Medes and Persians, nor yet those of the Macedonians have been able to enslave them.'
para3: By the 1st century BCE the kingdom was a power to be courted and feared: King Obodas I crushed the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus at Gadara in 93 BCE and slew the Seleucid king Antiochus XII in battle at Cana in 84, and was worshipped as a god after his death; under Aretas III and Aretas IV the realm reached its territorial and commercial zenith. But Rome was closing in: in 62 BCE Aretas III paid tribute to a Roman army at the gates of Petra, and the kingdom survived another century and a half as a wealthy Roman client state.
para4: The end came quietly: in 106 CE the emperor Trajan annexed the kingdom as the province of Arabia Petraea, and the caravan trade that had made the Nabataeans rich gradually shifted to other routes. Their legacy is written in stone - the treasury and tombs of Petra, carved whole from rose-red cliffs, and the waterworks that made a desert bloom - and in their script, which over the following centuries evolved into the Arabic alphabet used across the world today.

title: The Saka (Scythians)
titleline: The Saka (Scythians) - The History Web
para1: The Saka (Scythians). The Saka, known to the Greeks as Scythians, were an Eastern Iranic people of equestrian nomads who migrated from Central Asia - the steppes of what is now eastern Kazakhstan and the Altai-Sayan region - across the Araxes river to the Pontic Steppe north of the Black Sea in the 9th-8th centuries BCE. Their own name, Skuda, meant 'archers', and mounted archery was indeed the heart of their power: wherever they rode they left the same 'Scythian triad' of distinctive weapons, horse harness, and 'Animal Style' art, and gold pieces from the 8th-century BCE Arzhan kurgan show they were already master goldsmiths before they ever reached the west.
para2: In the 7th century BCE the Scythians crossed the Caucasus into West Asia, appearing in Assyrian records around 680 BCE as raiders, mercenaries, and then allies: King Bartatua married a daughter of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon in 672 BCE, making Scythia a nominal vassal of the empire. Under Bartatua's son Madyes, who helped Ashurbanipal crush the Babylonian revolt of 652 BCE, the Scythians imposed their hegemony on Media and began a nearly thirty-year supremacy in West Asia, conquering Urartu around 635 BCE and, alongside the Lydians, crushing the Cimmerians. The splendor of this age survives in their grave goods, where Assyrian and West Asian styles blend with steppe art.
para3: Around 600 BCE the Medes expelled the Scythians from West Asia, and they withdrew to the Pontic Steppe, their classic homeland. There they entered a golden age as partners of the Greek colonies dotting the Black Sea coast: Scythian grain, fish, furs, and slaves flowed south while Greek wine, pottery, and luxury goods flowed north, Greek craftsmen made gold and electrum vessels for Scythian nobles, and a mixed Graeco-Scythian culture flourished around Crimea. In 513 BCE the Persian king Darius I crossed the Danube with an enormous army to subdue them; Darius claimed victory, but the Greek tradition, following Herodotus, says the Scythians simply melted away before him, and the Greeks came to see the nomads as invincible.
para4: The Scythians dominated the western steppe until the 3rd century BCE, when their Sarmatian cousins conquered their lands, and the remnants were later overwhelmed by the Goths and absorbed into the peoples of the Migration Period. Their name outlived them so thoroughly that ancient, medieval, and early modern writers kept calling all sorts of unrelated steppe peoples 'Scythians'. Our fullest portrait comes from Herodotus, and their dazzling animal-style goldwork, much of it made for nomad chiefs by Greek craftsmen, remains among the treasures of the ancient world.

title: The Seleucids
titleline: The Seleucids - The History Web
para1: The Seleucids. The Seleucid Empire was the great Greek successor state of Alexander the Great's conquests in Asia, founded in 312 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander's generals, amid the Wars of the Diadochi that tore the dead conqueror's empire apart. From Babylonia, which he received in the partition of 321 and had to retake by force in 312, Seleucus built a realm stretching at its height from Anatolia to Central Asia and the borders of India - nearly four million square kilometers and over thirty million people. Victory at Ipsus in 301 BCE secured his Asian empire, ruled from the new cities he founded: Seleucia on the Tigris, then Antioch in Syria.
para2: The empire was the heartland of Hellenistic civilization: Greek was the official language, Greek settlers filled scores of new cities named for kings and queens, and an urban Greek elite formed the ruling class, while local traditions - Babylonian, Persian, Jewish - were generally tolerated beneath. Yet the empire faced both ways and strained at both ends. In the east, war with Chandragupta Maurya of India ended in 305 BCE with the cession of Alexander's Indus territories in exchange for alliance and war elephants; in the west, generations of Syrian Wars with Ptolemaic Egypt bled the kingdom for control of the Levant.
para3: The turning point came with Antiochus III the Great, who restored much of the empire's former reach but then marched into Greece and collided with Rome: defeated at Magnesia in 190 BCE, the Seleucids surrendered all lands west of the Taurus Mountains and paid crushing reparations. Worse, his successor Antiochus IV's attempt to force Greek customs on Judea provoked the Maccabean Revolt of 167 BCE, and while the kingdom was distracted, Mithridates I of Parthia swallowed its eastern heartlands, taking Babylon itself between 141 and 129 BCE, while the Greco-Bactrian kingdom flourished on its own in the northeast.
para4: Reduced by civil wars to a rump state in Syria, the once-great kingdom ended not with a bang but a signature: Tigranes the Great of Armenia took what was left in 83 BCE, and when the Roman general Pompey arrived in 63 BCE he simply annexed the remnants as the province of Syria. The Seleucid world outlived its dynasty, though - its Greek cities, its language, and its blend of Greek and Eastern cultures remained the fabric of the Near East for centuries, the world into which Rome stepped and in which much of later history would be written.

title: Xia Dynasty
titleline: Xia Dynasty - The History Web
para1: Xia Dynasty. The Xia dynasty (c. 2070-1600 BCE, by the conventional chronology) holds a unique place in Chinese history: it is the first dynasty of traditional Chinese historiography - and it may never have existed at all. The story as the Han historian Sima Qian and earlier classics tell it is a founding epic: when the Yellow River flooded catastrophically, the hero Yu the Great spent thirteen years taming the waters, digging channels to lead them to the sea, passing his own home three times without stopping. For this service the throne passed to him, and Yu founded the Xia - the first hereditary dynasty, replacing the age of sage-emperors who had chosen worthy successors.
para2: The problem is evidence. There are no contemporaneous written records of the Xia; the oldest Chinese writing, the Shang dynasty's oracle bones, never mentions them. The earliest mentions come in Zhou dynasty texts, centuries later - and those texts had an agenda, using the story of the Shang righteously replacing a corrupt Xia to justify their own replacement of the Shang. The traditional king list runs through seventeen rulers, ending with the tyrant Jie, whose cruelty - the story goes - cost the dynasty the Mandate of Heaven and let Tang of Shang overthrow it at the Battle of Mingtiao.
para3: Whether the Xia was history, legend, or something in between is one of Chinese archaeology's great open questions. Most Chinese archaeologists identify the Xia with the Erlitou culture (c. 1900-1500 BCE), whose excavated capital in Henan - with palace foundations, bronze workshops, and elite burials - was China's first state-level society, in the right place at roughly the right time. Many Western scholars remain unconvinced, noting that no Erlitou inscription names the Xia. The honest summary: a kingdom matching the traditional Xia in time and place existed; whether its people called themselves Xia is unknown.
para4: Legend or not, the Xia matters enormously, because it created the template of Chinese political legitimacy. The dynastic cycle - a virtuous founder, generations of decline, a corrupt last ruler who forfeits heaven's mandate, a righteous replacement - was constructed around the Xia-Shang-Zhou succession and governed how every later dynasty explained itself. China's story about where its civilization began begins with Yu and the flood, and that story shaped Chinese identity for two thousand years.

title: Xiongnu Confederation
titleline: Xiongnu Confederation - The History Web
para1: Xiongnu Confederation. The Xiongnu were the first great nomadic empire of the eastern Eurasian steppe: a tribal confederation that, from the 3rd century BCE, dominated the Mongolian Plateau and the grasslands from Siberia to the borders of China. Known to us mainly through Chinese histories - the Han historian Sima Qian devoted a chapter of his Records of the Grand Historian to them around 100 BCE - they were a multi-ethnic confederation whose language remains debated, with proposed links to Turkic, Mongolic, Iranian, and Yeniseian families, and possibly to the Huns who later appeared in the west.
para2: The founder of their empire was Modu Chanyu, who seized power from his father Touman in 209 BCE and welded the tribes into a disciplined state just as China itself was unified. Modu crushed the neighboring Donghu and drove out the Yuezhi - his son famously made a drinking cup from the Yuezhi king's skull - and in 200 BCE he trapped the first Han emperor, Gaozu, at Baideng with an army said to number 320,000. The humbled Han bought peace with the heqin system: princesses sent in marriage to the chanyu, annual gifts of silk, wine, and grain, and recognition of the Xiongnu as equals - in effect, tribute flowing north.
para3: The tide turned under Emperor Wu of Han, who abandoned appeasement in 133 BCE and sent his armies deep into the steppe. The campaigns of Wei Qing and Huo Qubing between 127 and 119 BCE retook the Ordos, shattered Xiongnu power south of the Gobi, and cost both sides terribly - one Han analysis records the Xiongnu losing 80-90,000 men, while fewer than 30,000 of the 140,000 Han horses came home. Weakened, the confederation tore itself apart in a civil war of rival chanyus, and in 53 BCE the southern chanyu Huhanye submitted to the Han, coming to Chang'an in person to pay homage - the mighty 'brotherly state' reduced to an outer vassal.
para4: The northern Xiongnu held out in the far west until Han armies and the rising Xianbei destroyed them in the late 1st century CE, and by the 7th century the Xiongnu had dissolved entirely into the peoples around them. Their descendants founded several of the Sixteen Kingdoms states in northern China, including Han-Zhao and Northern Liang. And their template - the mounted archer confederation binding the tribes into an empire that could face China as an equal - would be inherited by every steppe power that followed, down to the Turks and the Mongols.

title: Zhou Dynasty
titleline: Zhou Dynasty - The History Web
para1: Zhou Dynasty. The Zhou dynasty (c. 1046-256 BCE) ruled China longer than any dynasty before or since - nearly eight centuries - and though its kings wielded real power for less than a third of that span, the age they presided over created Chinese philosophy, Chinese political theory, and much of the classical canon. The Zhou began as a frontier people of the Wei River valley, culturally close to their Shang overlords, until King Wen built their strength and his son King Wu led the coalition that shattered the Shang at Muye around 1046 BCE.
para2: To rule the vast eastern plain, the early Zhou devised two instruments that defined China for millennia. The fengjian system parceled the realm into domains granted to royal kinsmen and allies - a feudal network binding far-flung colonies to the throne. And the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven explained why the Zhou, not the Shang, deserved to rule: heaven grants kingship to the virtuous and withdraws it from the corrupt, so conquest itself was proof of heaven's will. The Duke of Zhou, regent for the young King Cheng, crushed a great rebellion of the old Shang heartland and became Confucius's model of the virtuous statesman.
para3: Royal power lasted until 771 BCE, when nomadic Quanrong tribes sacked the capital Haojing and killed King You; the court fled east to Luoyang, and the 'Eastern Zhou' that followed was kingship in name only. The Spring and Autumn period (771-c. 481 BCE) saw dozens of states maneuver under a ceremonial Zhou king; the Warring States period (c. 475-221 BCE) that followed was total war - mass infantry armies, iron weapons, cavalry, and ruthless administrative reform - as the great states swallowed the small until only seven remained. Qin deposed the last Zhou king in 256 BCE and unified China by 221 BCE.
para4: Paradoxically, this age of collapse was China's greatest age of thought. As rival lords competed for talent, the 'Hundred Schools of Thought' flourished: Confucius taught a system of mutual duty and humane governance, Laozi and the Daoists counseled harmony with the natural Way, the Legalists demanded strict law and harsh punishment, Mozi preached universal care, and Sun Tzu codified the art of war. Chinese philosophy, statecraft, and ethics would live in the world the dying Zhou made for the next two thousand years.

title: Sumer and the Sumerian City-States
titleline: Sumer and the Sumerian City-States - The History Web
para1: Sumer and the Sumerian City-States. Sumer, the land of southern Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates (roughly modern southern Iraq), was home to the earliest known civilization in history. Settled from about 4500 BCE in the Ubaid period, the region's irrigation-fed farmland supported a dense network of cities by the fourth millennium: Eridu, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Nippur and others, each an independent city-state ruled from its temple and palace.
para2: The Sumerians produced an astonishing share of humanity's firsts. Around 3400-3200 BCE their accountants and priests developed cuneiform, the world's first writing system, first for grain tallies and then for law, literature and royal boasting. They built the ziggurat, worked bronze, used the potter's wheel and the wheeled cart, and organized math around the sixty-based numbers we still use for minutes and degrees. In the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900-2350 BCE) kings like Gilgamesh of Uruk and the royal tombs of Ur show a wealthy, competitive society of walled cities fighting over fields and canals.
para3: Sumer's cities fell to outside rulers - Sargon of Akkad around 2334 BCE, then the Gutians - but Sumerian civilization had one last brilliant chapter: the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112-2004 BCE), whose founder Ur-Nammu issued the earliest surviving law code and built the great ziggurat of Ur. When Amorite invaders and shifting rivers broke that kingdom, Sumer's political story ended, but its gods, epics and learning were absorbed wholesale by Babylon and Assyria.
para4: Every later Mesopotamian civilization, and through them much of the ancient world, built on Sumerian foundations: writing, law, kingship, the calendar, flood stories and school texts were still being copied in Sumerian a thousand years after the last Sumerian speaker died. The site's excavations in the 19th and 20th centuries recovered a whole lost civilization from the mounds of Iraq.

title: The Kingdom of Urartu
titleline: The Kingdom of Urartu - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Urartu. Urartu (c. 860-590 BCE), the biblical Ararat, was a powerful Iron Age kingdom centered on Lake Van in the mountainous highlands of eastern Anatolia, with lands reaching into modern Armenia and northwest Iran. Welded together from local tribes by King Sarduri I around 832 BCE, with its fortress capital at Tushpa (Van), it spent two and a half centuries as the northern rival of Assyria - the one neighbor the Assyrian kings could never permanently defeat.
para2: Urartu's kings, above all Menua and Argishti I, turned a harsh mountain land into an organized state. They built sophisticated irrigation works - the Menua Canal, still in use, carried water nearly 70 kilometers - terraced vineyards, and chains of spectacular hilltop fortresses like Erebuni (782 BCE, the nucleus of modern Yerevan) and Teishebaini. Urartian bronzesmiths and metalworkers produced armor, cauldrons and furniture traded across the Near East, and the royal chancery kept records in a cuneiform script of its own. Royal inscriptions boasted of building 'a marvel' wherever the kings campaigned, and archaeology has confirmed the boast.
para3: The kingdom's fate was tied to Assyria's. When Assyria was weak, Urartu expanded, even dictating terms to the states of northern Syria; when Sargon II marched north in 714 BCE and looted the holy city of Musasir, Urartu's confidence cracked. Pressure from Cimmerian and Scythian raiders from the steppe weakened it further, and after Assyria itself collapsed, the Medes overran the Urartian heartland around 590 BCE, burning its fortresses.
para4: Urartu vanished so completely that its memory survived mainly in Assyrian records and the Bible's 'mountains of Ararat', until 19th-century scholars deciphered its inscriptions. Its direct heir was Armenia: the Urartian language and people contributed heavily to the Armenian highland population, and the name of Yerevan descends from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Urartu

title: The Lydian and Phrygian Kingdoms
titleline: The Lydian and Phrygian Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Lydian and Phrygian Kingdoms. Phrygia and Lydia were the two great Iron Age kingdoms of western Anatolia, neighbors whose kings passed into Greek legend. The Phrygians, a people probably related to the Balkan Bryges, built their kingdom (c. 1200-700 BCE) on the ruins of the Hittite world with its capital at Gordium, where Midas - the historical King Mita of Assyrian records - ruled in the late 8th century and became the Greeks' golden-touch legend. Phrygian culture was distinctive: an early alphabet adapted from Phoenician, rock-cut monuments of the mountain mother goddess Matar (Cybele), and fine bronze and woodwork buried with their kings in huge tumulus tombs.
para2: Phrygia was smashed around 695 BCE by Cimmerian raiders from the steppe, and its western lands passed to Lydia. The Lydians, an Anatolian people with their capital at Sardis, rose under the Mermnad dynasty: Gyges, who took the throne around 680 BCE and fought the Cimmerians; then Ardys, Sadyattes, Alyattes, who pushed Lydian power to the Halys River and fought the Medes to a standstill in the famous 'Battle of the Eclipse' (585 BCE); and finally Croesus, whose name became a byword for wealth.
para3: Lydia's claim on history is money: the Lydians minted the world's first true coined currency, electrum and then pure gold and silver staters stamped with a royal lion, an invention that spread to Greece and Persia and changed trade forever. Croesus controlled the Greek cities of the Aegean coast and cultivated oracles across the Greek world, but in 546 BCE he misread Delphi's famous answer and marched on Cyrus the Great of Persia. Cyrus took Sardis, and Lydia became a Persian satrapy.
para4: Both kingdoms left deep marks on the Greeks who told their stories: Phrygia gave Greek religion Cybele and music its 'Phrygian mode', while Lydia gave it coinage, the tragic tale of Croesus and Solon, and its first great cautionary tale about pride and fortune.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Lydia and Phrygia

title: The Medes
titleline: The Medes - The History Web
para1: The Medes. The Medes were an Iranian people of the northwestern Zagros plateau (modern western Iran) who built the first great Iranian empire. Mentioned in Assyrian records from the 9th century BCE as tribute-paying chiefs, they were welded into a kingdom - tradition says by Deioces, who founded the capital at Ecbatana (modern Hamadan) - as Assyria's grip on the Iranian highlands weakened in the 7th century BCE.
para2: Under Cyaxares (r. 625-585 BCE) the Medes reorganized their army by weapon type, allied with Babylon, and in 614-612 BCE destroyed Assyria: Ashur fell in 614, and Nineveh itself was stormed and sacked in 612, an event that stunned the entire ancient world. The Medes took Assyria's northern and eastern provinces, fought Alyattes of Lydia to the 'Battle of the Eclipse' at the Halys in 585, and ruled an empire stretching from Anatolia across Iran toward Central Asia.
para3: The empire was short-lived. Cyaxares' son Astyages ruled for about 35 years, but in 550 BCE his own vassal, Cyrus of the Persian kingdom of Anshan, rebelled; the Median army defected, Ecbatana was taken, and the Median Empire became the heartland of Cyrus' new Persian (Achaemenid) Empire. Median nobles kept high office under the Persians - the pair 'Medes and Persians' became a standard phrase - and two later Median revolts tried and failed to restore the kingdom. Ecbatana remained one of the Achaemenid summer capitals, and 'Median' dress and court customs visibly shaped Persian royal style.
para4: Little Median writing survives, so the Medes are seen mostly through Assyrian, Babylonian, Greek and later Persian sources, and their archaeology (Ecbatana, Godin Tepe, Nush-i Jan) is still being worked out. But their historical role is clear: they broke Assyria, taught the Persians the arts of empire, and gave Iranian civilization its first imperial form.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 4.2: From Old Babylon to the Medes

title: The Parthian Empire
titleline: The Parthian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Parthian Empire. The Parthian Empire (247 BCE-224 CE) was founded when Arsaces I, chief of the Parni nomads, seized the province of Parthia from the crumbling Seleucid Empire and made himself king. His dynasty, the Arsacids, spent a century consolidating the Iranian plateau before Mithridates I (r. 171-132 BCE) took Media, Babylonia and the great city of Seleucia in 141 BCE, making Parthia the heir to Persia and the master of the lands between the Euphrates and the Indus.
para2: For nearly four centuries Parthia was Rome's equal and its only lasting rival. The Parthians' horse archers and armored cataphracts destroyed Crassus and his legions at Carrhae in 53 BCE - Rome's worst defeat in the east - and later saw off invasions by Mark Antony and several emperors, though Trajan and others did sack the capital Ctesiphon (opposite Seleucia on the Tigris) when Parthian politics turned chaotic. Between the two empires ran the Silk Road, and Parthian control of its western end made the empire rich on the China-Rome trade.
para3: The empire was a loose, almost feudal structure: the 'King of Kings' ruled through powerful noble houses like the Suren and Karen, semi-independent vassal kingdoms, and Greek and Mesopotamian cities with their own privileges. Its culture mixed Iranian, Greek, Babylonian and steppe elements - Greek was used on early coins, Zoroastrianism grew stronger over time, and Parthian art developed its own distinctive front-facing style seen at Hatra and Dura-Europos.
para4: Constant civil wars over the succession wore the Arsacids down. In 224 CE Ardashir I, a vassal king from Persis (Fars), defeated and killed the last Parthian king Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan and founded the Sasanian Empire. But the great Parthian families survived as pillars of the Sasanian aristocracy, and Parthia's four centuries had set the pattern of Iranian kingship that its successors inherited.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Parthian Empire (247 B.C.-224 A.D.)

title: The Sasanian Empire
titleline: The Sasanian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Sasanian Empire. The Sasanian Empire (224-651 CE) was the last and most glorious of the pre-Islamic Iranian empires. It was founded by Ardashir I, a king of Persis who overthrew his Parthian overlord in 224 and rebuilt Iranian kingship around his dynasty, Zoroastrian orthodoxy, and a centralized administration. His son Shapur I made the young empire a superpower: in 260 he defeated the Romans at Edessa and captured the emperor Valerian alive - a humiliation carved on the royal rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam - and pushed Persian arms to the Mediterranean.
para2: For four centuries the Sasanians were Rome's and then Byzantium's great rival. Wars over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the trade routes see-sawed for generations, punctuated by long peace treaties. At home the kings built cities, canals and fire temples; Zoroastrianism became a state church, while Manichaeism appeared and was suppressed and Christian, Jewish and Buddhist communities lived under varying tolerance. The reign of Khosrow I Anushirvan ('of the immortal soul', r. 531-579) was the empire's golden age: tax and military reforms, the academy of Gondishapur where Greek, Persian, Syrian and Indian learning met, and a reputation for justice that made him a model king in later Islamic literature.
para3: Khosrow II (r. 590-628) gambled on total victory: his armies took Jerusalem (614), Egypt (619) and camped opposite Constantinople, but the emperor Heraclius struck back, shattered the Persian army at Nineveh (627), and the empire collapsed into palace coups - eight rulers in four years. Exhausted and divided, the Sasanians could not withstand the armies of the Muslim conquest: Qadisiyya (636) and Nahavand (642) decided the war, and the last king, Yazdegerd III, was killed at Merv in 651.
para4: The Sasanian legacy was enormous. Its court ceremony, titles, silver, textiles and art were copied from Byzantium to China; its scholars preserved Greek and Indian science for the Islamic world; and its model of centralized, cosmopolitan kingship became the template the Abbasid caliphs followed in Iraq.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Sasanian Empire (224-651 A.D.)

title: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
titleline: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom (c. 256-125 BCE) was the easternmost outpost of the Hellenistic world: a Greek-ruled state in Bactria and Sogdiana (northern Afghanistan and southern Central Asia), a thousand kilometers beyond the other successor kingdoms of Alexander the Great. Its founder, the satrap Diodotus I, broke away from the Seleucid Empire around 256 BCE, and his son Diodotus II was overthrown by Euthydemus I, who famously defended the kingdom's independence against Antiochus III's siege of Bactra (208-206 BCE).
para2: Under Demetrius I (r. c. 200-180 BCE) the Greco-Bactrians crossed the Hindu Kush and conquered northwestern India, founding a whole family of Indo-Greek kingdoms. Their cities were full Greek poleis planted in Central Asia: Ai-Khanoum, on the Oxus, had a theater, a gymnasium, Greek inscriptions of Delphic maxims, and a palace blending Greek and Persian forms. Their kings minted superb silver portraits - among the finest coins ever struck - with Greek on one side and local scripts on the other.
para3: The kingdom's later history was fractious. Eucratides, a rival king, overthrew the Euthydemids around 170 BCE, civil wars multiplied claimants, and the realm split between rulers north and south of the Hindu Kush. Around 145-125 BCE nomad peoples on the move - Sakas and the Yuezhi, the future Kushans - overran Bactria, and the last Greek kings north of the mountains disappeared, though their Indo-Greek cousins ruled in Pakistan and India into the early 1st century CE.
para4: Greco-Bactria matters far beyond its size: it carried Greek art and institutions deep into Asia, created the Greco-Buddhist fusion that produced Gandhara art and the first anthropomorphic images of the Buddha, and sat astride the routes that soon became the Silk Road, linking China, India and the Mediterranean. The Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda), remembered in Buddhist tradition as the wise questioner of the monk Nagasena, shows how thoroughly these Greek rulers entered the Asian world they had conquered.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: BACTRIA i. Pre-Islamic period

title: The Kushan Empire
titleline: The Kushan Empire - The History Web
para1: The Kushan Empire. The Kushan Empire (c. 30-375 CE) was built by the Yuezhi, a nomadic confederation driven west from the borders of China, who settled in Bactria and were united into an empire by Kujula Kadphises. His successors pressed south: Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises took the Indus region, and under Kanishka I the Kushans ruled a vast realm from the Central Asian steppe through Afghanistan to the Ganges plain, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura. Kanishka's accession (dated variously to 127, or more recently 127-151 CE by most scholars) marks the empire's peak.
para2: The Kushans sat at the crossroads of the ancient world. Their territory straddled the Silk Road, and Roman gold, Indian ivory, Chinese silk and Central Asian horses all passed through their markets - Kushan gold coins imitated Roman weight standards. Their court was famously cosmopolitan: coins show Greek, Iranian, Indian and steppe gods labeled in Greek and Bactrian script, and Kanishka's era was used for centuries across South and Central Asia.
para3: The Kushans' greatest cultural legacy is Buddhist. Kanishka is remembered in Buddhist tradition as a second Ashoka: he is credited with convening the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, and under Kushan patronage Buddhism spread along the trade routes into Central Asia and China. The Gandhara and Mathura schools of art flourished under them, producing the first human images of the Buddha and the giant statues of Bamiyan's artistic ancestors.
para4: From the early 3rd century the empire declined: Ardashir I and the Sasanians took Bactria (making the western Kushans their vassal 'Kushanshahs'), while the Gupta kings absorbed the Indian provinces. Reduced to a rump in the Kabul valley, the last Kushans were finally overwhelmed by the Kidarite Huns around 375. But for three centuries they had linked China, India, Iran and Rome into one commercial and cultural world.

title: The Satavahana Dynasty
titleline: The Satavahana Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Satavahana Dynasty. The Satavahanas (c. 1st century BCE-early 3rd century CE) were the first great indigenous dynasty of the Deccan, ruling the plateau of south-central India from capitals at Pratishthana (Paithan) and later Amaravati. Appearing in the aftermath of the Mauryan Empire's collapse, they built a kingdom that stretched at its height from sea to sea across peninsular India and fought off the foreign powers of the northwest - the Shakas (Western Kshatrapas), and by extension the legacies of the Indo-Greeks and Kushans.
para2: The dynasty's finest hour came under Gautamiputra Satakarni (r. c. 106-130), who crushed the Western Kshatrapas and restored Satavahana power from Malwa to the Coromandel coast - his mother proudly recorded his victories in a famous Nashik inscription. His successors Vashishtiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni kept the kingdom prosperous, and Satavahana ports like Kalyan shipped cotton, spices and gems to the Roman world - Roman coins are found across the Deccan, and Pliny complained of the drain of Roman gold to India.
para3: The Satavahanas ruled a diverse, largely tolerant state. They performed Vedic sacrifices and claimed Brahmin status, but gave lavishly to Buddhist monks: the great stupa complexes of Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Sanchi's gateways were built or enriched under their rule, and their inscriptions are in Prakrit written in Brahmi script. Land grants to Buddhist monasteries recorded in their inscriptions are among the earliest of their kind in India.
para4: In the 3rd century the dynasty fragmented into local successor states - the Ikshvakus, Abhiras and Vakatakas - but its model endured. The Satavahanas had opened the Deccan to settled kingdoms, maritime trade and Sanskrit and Prakrit court culture, and the artistic traditions they sponsored, above all Amaravati sculpture, became a foundation of later South Indian art.

title: The Hung Kings and Van Lang
titleline: The Hung Kings and Van Lang - The History Web
para1: The Hung Kings and Van Lang. The Hung Kings (Vua Hung) are the legendary founders of Vietnam: eighteen rulers of the Hong Bang dynasty said to have reigned over Van Lang, a kingdom of the Lac Viet people in the Red River delta of northern Vietnam, from the mythical date of 2879 BCE until 258 BCE. Though the traditional chronology belongs to legend rather than documented history, the Hung Kings stand at the head of the Vietnamese national story - every later dynasty claimed descent from them, and their commemoration is a national holiday in Vietnam today.
para2: Behind the legends lies a real Bronze Age world. Van Lang, organized into districts and led by military chiefs and scholars under the Hung king, coincides in time and place with the Dong Son culture (c. 1000 BCE-1st century CE), famous for its magnificent bronze drums decorated with boats, warriors and festivals - the finest bronze tradition of ancient Southeast Asia. Dong Son society was a rice-growing, riverine civilization in regular contact with the Dong Dau and Go Mun cultures and with the expanding Chinese world to the north.
para3: In 258 BCE Van Lang was taken over by Thuc Phan (An Duong Vuong), a neighboring ruler who merged it with his own land of Au Lac and built the great spiral citadel of Co Loa near modern Hanoi - the largest prehistoric fortress of Southeast Asia. His kingdom soon fell to the Zhao general Zhao Tuo's Nanyue, and in 111 BCE the armies of Han China conquered the region outright, beginning a thousand years of Chinese rule.
para4: The Hung Kings' significance is national rather than documentary: as the mythic first state of the Vietnamese, Van Lang gave Vietnam a founding story distinct from China's, and the cult of the Hung Kings at their temple in Phu Tho remains a living symbol of Vietnamese identity.

title: The Warring States Period
titleline: The Warring States Period - The History Web
para1: The Warring States Period. The Warring States period (475-221 BCE) was the age of total war that ended ancient China's Zhou order and forged its first empire. As the Zhou kings lost all real power, their former vassal states devoured each other; after the partition of the great state of Jin in 403 BCE, seven major powers - Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei - fought for supremacy across the Chinese world for over two centuries.
para2: Warfare was transformed. Small aristocratic chariot armies gave way to mass infantry levies numbering in the hundreds of thousands, armed with iron weapons and the deadly crossbow, while the northern states learned cavalry from the steppe nomads. Victory went to the states that reformed most ruthlessly: Shang Yang's Legalist reforms in Qin (from 356 BCE) replaced hereditary privilege with military merit, strict law, and registration of the whole population, turning Qin into the most efficient war machine of the age.
para3: The same violent century was China's greatest age of thought - the Hundred Schools of Philosophy. Confucians like Mencius and Xunzi, Daoists like Zhuangzi, the Legalists Han Fei and Li Si, Mohists, logicians and strategists all debated how to restore order, and their answers became the permanent furniture of Chinese civilization. Diplomacy ('vertical and horizontal' alliances), trade, city growth and iron-fueled agriculture flourished even as the battles - like Changping in 260 BCE, where Qin buried alive tens of thousands of Zhao prisoners - grew ever more terrible.
para4: The end came fast: Qin's king Ying Zheng destroyed Han (230), Zhao (228), Wei (225), Chu (223), Yan (222) and finally Qi (221), uniting China and proclaiming himself First Emperor. The Warring States period had created the centralized bureaucratic empire - and the philosophical traditions - that would define China for two thousand years.
