title: The Qin Dynasty
titleline: The Qin Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Qin Dynasty. The Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) lasted only fifteen years, but it created China. In 221 BCE Ying Zheng, king of the western state of Qin, completed the conquest of his six rivals and took a new title - Qin Shi Huang, First August Emperor of Qin - ruling the first unified empire in Chinese history. Guided by his chancellor Li Si and Legalist doctrine, he abolished the old feudal states and divided the empire into thirty-six commanderies governed by appointed officials.
para2: The First Emperor standardized a civilization. One script, one currency, one set of weights and measures, one axle width for carts were imposed across the empire; great roads radiated from the capital Xianyang; and hundreds of thousands of laborers joined the old northern walls into the first Great Wall against the steppe, while armies pushed south to the coasts of Guangdong. His suspicion of criticism produced the infamous 'burning of the books' (213 BCE) and the burying of scholars - though practical and court texts were preserved.
para3: His megalomania built his own tomb: an underground palace-city east of Xianyang guarded by the Terracotta Army, some eight thousand life-size soldier statues discovered by farmers in 1974, now among the most famous archaeological finds on earth. When the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, a palace conspiracy put his weak younger son on the throne; within a year the empire exploded in peasant and aristocratic revolts (209 BCE), and by 206 the Qin was destroyed.
para4: Yet the Qin did not really fail: the Han dynasty that replaced it kept almost its entire system - centralized bureaucracy, commanderies, standardized law and script - for four centuries, and every Chinese empire since has been built on the Qin template. Even China's English name comes from 'Qin'.
source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Qin Dynasty (221-206 B.C.)
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 5.4: The Qin Dynasty

title: The Han Dynasty
titleline: The Han Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Han Dynasty. The Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) was China's first great golden age, so central to Chinese identity that the Chinese still call themselves 'people of Han'. Its founder, Liu Bang - a commoner and minor official - won the civil wars after Qin's fall and ruled as Emperor Gaozu, establishing his capital at Chang'an. His successors of the Western Han consolidated the empire, restoring moderate taxes and peace after Qin's exhaustion while keeping its centralized administration.
para2: Under Emperor Wu (r. 141-87 BCE), the 'Martial Emperor', Han China became the largest and richest state on earth. His armies broke the Xiongnu nomad confederation of the steppe, seized the Hexi Corridor, and planted garrisons in Central Asia; his envoy Zhang Qian's journey to the west opened the Silk Road linking China to Persia and Rome. At home Wu made Confucianism the state ideology, founded an imperial university, and established state monopolies on salt and iron to pay for the wars.
para3: After a brief interruption - the reformer-usurper Wang Mang's Xin dynasty (9-25 CE) - the Later or Eastern Han reigned from Luoyang for another two centuries of prosperity: paper was presented at court in 105 CE, Buddhism entered China, and scholars compiled the great histories. But the dynasty slowly rotted from within as palace eunuchs and empresses' clans fought for control, great landowning families swallowed the tax-paying peasantry, and the devastating Yellow Turban Rebellion (184) forced the court to arm regional warlords it could no longer command.
para4: The warlord Cao Cao held the last emperor as a puppet, and in 220 his son Cao Pi formally ended the Han, opening the age of the Three Kingdoms. But the Han model - a Confucian bureaucracy ruling a unified agrarian empire - became China's permanent ideal, matched in world history only by contemporary Rome.

source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Han Dynasty

title: The Yamato and Kofun Periods
titleline: The Yamato and Kofun Periods - The History Web
para1: The Yamato and Kofun Periods. The Kofun ('old tomb') period (c. 250-538 CE) takes its name from the gigantic keyhole-shaped burial mounds raised for Japan's rulers - the largest, the Daisenryo mound near Osaka traditionally assigned to Emperor Nintoku, is one of the biggest tombs in the world, ringed by moats and guarded by thousands of haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses and houses. These monuments mark the rise of the Yamato court in central Japan, the dynasty that still occupies the Japanese throne.
para2: The Yamato kings (uji no kami, later tenno) were first among the chieftains of a loose confederation of clans (uji), each with its own lands, gods and crafts. Power rested on control of rice land, iron, and the 'be' groups of hereditary artisans - weavers, smiths, scribes and horsemen, many of them immigrants from Korea and China. Iron tools and weapons transformed agriculture and war, and mounted warriors in the 5th century strengthened the court's grip.
para3: Yamato Japan was in constant contact with the mainland: the 'Five Kings of Wa' sent embassies to Chinese courts in the 5th century and received titles from them, while armies intervened in the wars of the Korean kingdoms and maintained a foothold at Mimana (Gaya). From Korea came writing, iron technology, and eventually, in 538 or 552 CE, a gift of Buddhist images and sutras from the king of Baekje - the arrival of Buddhism, conventionally ending the Kofun and opening the Asuka period.
para4: In the 7th century the Yamato court reorganized itself on Chinese models - the Taika Reforms of 645, the ritsuryo codes, and the first permanent capital at Nara (710) - transforming a confederation of clans into a centralized imperial state. The kofun themselves remain the period's great witnesses: still unexcavated out of respect for the imperial ancestors, their haniwa and grave goods preserve the look of Japan's first kingdom.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Kofun Period (ca. 300-710)

title: The Three Kingdoms of Korea
titleline: The Three Kingdoms of Korea - The History Web
para1: The Three Kingdoms of Korea. The Three Kingdoms period (traditionally 57 BCE-668 CE) shaped the Korean nation. Three rival states divided the peninsula: Goguryeo, a warlike kingdom of horsemen in the northern mountains and Manchuria; Baekje in the southwest, a maritime power with close ties to Japan; and Silla in the southeast, the most isolated and conservative of the three. A small confederation, Gaya, held the southern tip between Baekje and Silla until Silla absorbed it in 562.
para2: The 4th and 5th centuries were Goguryeo's age of glory: its king Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391-413) - whose giant inscribed stele still stands in Manchuria - conquered deep into Manchuria and south down the peninsula. All three kingdoms adopted Chinese writing, administration and Buddhism (Goguryeo 372, Baekje 384, Silla 527), building a cultured aristocratic civilization of walled cities, gilded temples and tombs filled with gold crowns and murals of the four directional guardians. Baekje in turn passed writing, crafts and Buddhism to the early Japanese court.
para3: From the 6th century Silla rose, fighting a long duel with Goguryeo for the peninsula's center. The decisive turn was diplomatic: Silla allied with Tang China, and the allies destroyed Baekje (660) and then Goguryeo (668) - which had famously beaten off massive invasions by the Sui dynasty decades earlier. Silla then expelled its own Tang allies from the peninsula by 676, ruling a unified Korea south of the Taedong River.
para4: Unified Silla's centuries of peace, with its capital at Gyeongju - 'the museum without walls' - saw the flowering of Buddhist art at Bulguksa and the Seokguram grotto. The Three Kingdoms era had defined Korea's language, territory, Buddhism and identity: later Koreans looked back to these kingdoms, especially Goguryeo, as the wellsprings of the nation.

source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Samguk Sagi

title: The Kingdoms of Ancient Yemen
titleline: The Kingdoms of Ancient Yemen - The History Web
para1: The Kingdoms of Ancient Yemen. In antiquity Yemen was Arabia Felix - 'Happy Arabia' - the one corner of the peninsula blessed with monsoon rains and terraced highland farms, and above all with frankincense and myrrh, the precious resins whose caravans made southwest Arabia rich. From about 1000 BCE a series of literate kingdoms rose there: Saba (Sheba), Ma'in, Qataban, Hadhramawt and Awsan, each with its own gods, temples and monumental inscriptions in the South Arabian script.
para2: Greatest of them was Saba, the kingdom of the biblical Queen of Sheba, whose power rested on the Ma'rib Dam - one of the engineering wonders of the ancient world, a great stone barrier that watered thousands of hectares of gardens. Sabaean caravans carried incense up the length of Arabia to Gaza and Damascus, making the kingdom famous from the Bible to Herodotus. The kingdoms' temples, tower-houses and alabaster statues show a sophisticated urban civilization wholly distinct from the desert around it.
para3: In the late 3rd century CE the highland kingdom of Himyar absorbed its rivals, including Saba, uniting Yemen under one rule. Himyar's kings converted from the old paganism to Judaism, and the kingdom became a battleground of empires and faiths: when King Dhu Nuwas massacred the Christians of Najran (c. 523), the Christian kingdom of Aksum (Ethiopia) invaded with Byzantine blessing, conquered Himyar in 525, and its viceroy Abraha ruled Yemen - and, tradition says, marched on Mecca in the Year of the Elephant, the year of the Prophet Muhammad's birth.
para4: Persian Sasanian troops expelled the Ethiopians around 570, and Yemen passed under Persian and then Muslim rule. The final breaching of the Ma'rib Dam became an Arabic proverb for the scattering of a nation. But the incense kingdoms left Arabia's only ancient urban civilization, and their ruins - and the dam, rebuilt in 1986 - remain Yemen's great monuments.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Saba
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: ARABIA ii. The Sasanians and Arabia

title: The Ghassanids and the Lakhmids
titleline: The Ghassanids and the Lakhmids - The History Web
para1: The Ghassanids and the Lakhmids. The Ghassanids and Lakhmids were two Arab kingdoms that dominated the frontiers of the 6th-century Near East: the Ghassanids as clients (foederati) of Byzantium on the Syrian steppe, the Lakhmids as clients of Sasanian Persia at al-Hira on the desert edge of Iraq. Both were Arab tribal dynasties - the Ghassanids tracing their origin to emigrants from Yemen, the Lakhmids to the Tanukh - and their rivalry, fought out in proxy wars and poetry, was the Arabian theater of the great Roman-Persian duel.
para2: The Ghassanids guarded Byzantium's desert frontier against raiders and against the Lakhmids, supplied elite cavalry to imperial armies, and were rewarded with royal titles; their greatest king, al-Harith ibn Jabalah (Arethas), was honored by Justinian himself and defeated the Lakhmids at the battle of Qinnasrin (554). Deeply loyal to Miaphysite Christianity, the Ghassanid court sheltered its theologians and monks, and their palaces, churches and camps - from Jabiya in the Golan to Sergiopolis (Resafa) - dotted the Syrian steppe.
para3: The Lakhmids ruled at al-Hira for some three centuries as the shield of the Sasanian kings, keeping the desert Arabs in check and raiding Byzantine Syria. Their capital became the cultural capital of pre-Islamic Arabia: Arab poets sang at its court, Christian monks and bishops flourished under its protection, and it was there that Arabic, still largely a spoken language, began to be written down. In 602 Khosrow II treacherously deposed and killed the last Lakhmid king, al-Nu'man III, abolishing the dynasty - and the border Arabs, answering with their victory over the Persians at Dhi Qar, showed what the Persians had lost.
para4: Both kingdoms crumbled before the Muslim conquests of the 630s: the Ghassanids fought for Byzantium at the Yarmuk (636) and faded into the new order, while Hira surrendered and its people joined the conquerors. Together they had carried Arab tribal society, language and poetry to the edge of statehood - the immediate prelude to the rise of Islam.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: LAKHMIDS

title: The Hattians
titleline: The Hattians - The History Web
para1: The Hattians. The Hattians were the earliest known civilization of central Anatolia (modern Turkey), flourishing in the 3rd millennium BCE before the arrival of the Indo-European Hittites who later took their land and their name. They spoke Hattic, a language unrelated to any known family, and their network of fortified cities - Hattusa, Alaca Hoyuk, Kanesh and others - ruled the Anatolian plateau at the dawn of the Bronze Age.
para2: Everything known of the Hattians comes from archaeology and from the records of their neighbors. The royal tombs of Alaca Hoyuk (c. 2500-2300 BCE), with their gold and bronze standards of stags and bulls, sun-disc ornaments and rich metalwork, reveal a wealthy aristocratic society already trading across the Near East. Around 1900 BCE Assyrian merchants planted a trading colony (karum) at Kanesh, and its thousands of cuneiform tablets - the oldest written documents from Anatolia - show Hattian cities as partners and rivals in the international metals trade.
para3: From around 2000-1700 BCE Indo-European speakers - the Hittites - moved into the plateau, absorbing Hattian cities and culture. Hattusa became the Hittite capital; the early Hittite king even took the throne name Hattusili, 'man of Hattusa'. The Hattic language died out as a living tongue but survived for centuries in Hittite temples as a sacred ceremonial language, and Hattian gods - above all the sun goddess of Arinna, the Hittites' chief deity - formed the core of the later Hittite pantheon.
para4: The Hattians' memory was so thoroughly absorbed by their successors that they were forgotten until modern archaeology uncovered Alaca Hoyuk and the Hittite archives distinguished the older 'Hattic' layer beneath. They stand as the first chapter of Anatolia's long history, the foundation on which the Hittite Empire - and through it the history of the Near East - was built.
